name: The Fisherman and the Banker
description:
85 min | Gujarati, Kutchi, Hindi and English with English subtitles 
A modern-day David and Goliath tale, this documentary chronicles the Wagher fishermen of Gujarat as they fight against industrial encroachment. They take on the World Bank’s private lending arm, the International Finance Corporation (IFC), for funding a coal-fired power plant that threatens their way of life. A groundbreaking lawsuit, filed with the support of US lawyers, reaches the US Supreme Court in 2018. With a poetic and observational lens, the film explores their legal battle and profound bond with the environment, posing a powerful question: can the resilience of a community rewrite the rules of global power?

name: Enchantment
description:
Shaped by Pandit Ravi Shankar’s own witty and poignant words, Enchantment is a theatrical journey into the mind of the sitar maestro, weaving theatre, live dance and music into a richly immersive experience. Instead of a standard retelling of the global icon’s legendary career, this bioplay steps into the inner world of his doubts, regrets, struggles, and the fiery resolve that carried him from a boy dancer in Paris to one of the most influential musicians of the 20th century. Through moments of vulnerability and brilliance, the play reveals how Ravi Shankar transformed adversity into artistic triumph. 
The journey passes through the four stages in his life: 

the boy in Paris, acclaimed as a dancer in his brother’s troupe
the disciple undergoing relentless training in music in a remote Indian town
the zealous artist struggling to establish a career
the global icon, putting Indian music on the world map.

Written and directed by Gowri Ramnarayan, the production features Ravi Shankar’s original sitar recordings, and also some of his own compositions, rendered exclusively for Enchantment by lead vocalist Bombay Jayashri, with Aditya Prakash and Vignesh Ishwar. Premiered in Chennai in September 2025, this widely acclaimed play has just completed a coast-to-coast US Tour with 15 shows. 
Director’s Note
 
Every play begins with a question. Enchantment asks – how do you conjure up a legendary artist of your own times on the stage, whose life has been exhaustively documented on page and screen? 
Only if I relied on personal interactions over the years with the maestro, and his partner of 24 years, Kamala Chakravarti, and my interviews with him as a journalist. I had to focus on the protagonist’s doubts and regrets to transform biography into the universal human struggle to survive, to succeed. I could use dance, and the maestro’s own
music to convey what words cannot express. 
Two actors. Two dancers. A lighting person. They actualise an entire life story. The stage showcases a superstar. But audiences see a human being whose vulnerabilities are their own.

name: To Die a Frenchman
description:
80 min | Tamil with English Subtitles | 2026 | India 
Monsieur Mounissamy is a seventy-year-old man living in the crumbling neighbourhood of Ville Noir in Pondicherry, where French street names fade into dust and memories of empire linger. Each July 14th, French National Day, he unfurls a flag mirroring the French tricolour and sings, in trembling, imperfect French, an anthem to a “Mother France” he believes could still reclaim him. He spends his life fighting for French citizenship and a tiny plot of Indian land, anchoring himself in histories that abandoned him. What do we call those who never crossed a border, yet woke up one day to find themselves citizens of a country they did not choose? 
When colonial France withdrew from Pondicherry without a plebiscite, it disregarded its own constitutional principles, and native Tamils became unintended bystanders in a political contest between two nations. Mounissamy’s longing for French citizenship was not merely a legal pursuit, but an attempt to reclaim an identity stolen from him. Shot over five years, this cinematic elegy looks beyond Pondicherry’s romanticised French facade to confront colonialism, citizenship and belonging. 
The screening will be followed by a discussion between Pankaj Rishi Kumar, the director and Ramjee Chandran. The session will end with an audience Q&A. 
This event is part of a double bill of films exploring French colonial histories, memories and their lasting legacies. We invite you to join us for both screenings. View the accompanying film here.

name: BUILD
description:
Sticks, clay, sound, and rhythm come together in this non-verbal theatre performance. 
BUILD is about the joy of discovery and the freedom of imaginative play. Through hands-on engagement in a safe, welcoming space, the performance offers children and parents a chance to reconnect with nature and rediscover the play of a bygone era. 
Inspired by the open-ended games children invent when left to their own devices, Two young performers explore the possibilities of play away from screens and digital distractions. One with sticks and the other with clay, together they discover different sizes, colours, textures and shapes as they create, connect, and find their own rhythm along the way.

name: Leading Climate Action from the Ground Up
description:
Who decides how to run the Western Ghats? 
This panel discussion examines the emerging frames in climate communication, and the public outcry they generate. Specifically, the policy imbroglio over declaring the Western Ghats a World Heritage Site, which is yet to reach a decisive point. Through case studies of Kodagu and Chikmagalur, two economically rich districts of Karnataka, the discussion examines community and citizen activism, alongside the role and impact of social media. 
The Central Government has recently reissued its draft notification proposing an Ecologically Sensitive Zone across the Western Ghats, after the previous draft lapsed amid continuing differences between the six states it traverses. Ambiguity in policy and legislation can lead to skewed development, often at the cost of fragile biodiversity and the communities that depend on it. The discussion also outlines the essential role offline, on-ground efforts play in mediating policy, legislation and community action.

name: PCOS? PCOD? PMOS! – What’s in a Name?
description:
Poly Cystic Ovarian Syndrome, or Poly Cystic Ovarian Disease, has long struck fear into the hearts of young women and their anxious parents. This talk unpacks the physiology of ovarian function, exploring why it occurs, why it affects other systems in the body, and what its long-term consequences really are. Recently renamed Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Disease, the condition is entering a new chapter of understanding. Why is this a welcome change? 
When people understand how their bodies work, they’re better equipped to take care of their own health. Aimed at empowering young women, people with a uterus and ovaries, and their supporters, the session explores whether there is a cure and if lifestyle changes can really make a difference.

name: Fire Drawing Workshop
description:
Have you ever played with fire? 
In this hands-on workshop participants learn a technique the artist has spent five years developing: burning or “fuming” wood with matches, candles, and pyrography tools to create textured, tonal, almost painterly images. The process allows partial control over the outcome, producing fine relief-like details and layered effects akin to glazing with flame. 
Fire is at the heart of creation, alongside wood and the artist’s own hands, in a slow, attentive dialogue between intention and element. Participants will experiment directly with flame and wood, exploring a completely new material language while reconnecting with something older: attentiveness to matter, to process, and to the natural world.

name: Tiger Man, Burning Bright!
description:
Can the recovery of a single species hold the key to saving creatures across an entire continent? 
Based on Tiger Memories: My Life in Wildlife Conservation by K. Ullas Karanth, this panel discussion traces the history and social context of tiger conservation in India and Asia over the past six decades. The conversation illustrates the centrality of rigorous wildlife science to effective conservation, combining top-down and bottom-up approaches from field biology and statistical ecology, and explores the future prospects for tigers and wild nature in a wider socio-environmental context. 
Coauthored with naturalist Joshua Mathew and published by Penguin Random House India, the book illustrates Karanth’s wildlife adventures, pioneering research, and passionate battles to save big cats and wild nature. It traces his long career studying and conserving wild tigers, from exploring the forests of Karnataka’s Malenad as a teenager to becoming one of the world’s leading wildlife biologists.

name: Celebrating Nisar in Word and Song
description:
Over five decades of prodigious poetic output, the late Padma Shri KS Nisar Ahmed (1936-2020), one of Karnataka’s most beloved contemporary poets, captured both the minutiae of daily life and the spirit of the age in verses that are as provocative as they are deeply lyrical. Steeped in both Romantic and Modernist traditions, his work blends intellectual rigour with heartfelt emotion, remaining strikingly relevant across generations. Every Day a Celebration gathers some of the Nityotsava Kavi’s finest poems, and introduces his voice to a wider audience and a new generation through Roopa Pai’s sensitive translation. 
Many of Nisar’s poems were set to music, which made them even more familiar and dear to Kannada audiences at home and abroad. 
Believing that the best way to celebrate and honour Nisar’s legacy is to have the audience experience his work through both word and song, this event incorporates both in equal measure. The conversation between Roopa Pai and Aleemulla Khan will be interspersed with performances of the songs, and conclude with interaction with the audience.

description:

Mahé is a small, former French colony on the Malabar Coast of India. It carries a layered history shaped by colonial encounters, migration, language, memory, and cultural exchange. The film asks what remains of the French presence in Mahé today, through honest conversations, surreal landscapes and lived experiences. Why do colonial histories continue to inhabit everyday life long after political rule has ended? 
Départ is an attempt to understand what remains when an entire chapter of history has passed, and what is quietly lost when the last voices capable of telling that story fall silent. The film invites audiences to look beyond the familiar narratives of colonialism, toward the quieter, more intimate ways history survives in places, communities, identities, and memories.

name: The Future of Protest
description:
Humour is reshaping political imagination. 
This discussion explores the frustrations driving young people towards political action, why established political channels may feel inadequate, and how humour, memes and digital culture become tools of subversion and power. The recent protests around competitive examinations, and the emergence of phenomena such as the satirical Cockroach Party, have brought these currents dramatically into public view. Humour and memes are becoming Gen Z’s political vocabulary, filling a gap that conventional politics has left behind 
Young people have always been at the forefront of protest movements, and humour, music and irreverence have long histories as tools of dissent. This session illuminates what is genuinely new about this moment, with the capacity to create narratives, symbols, satire and online communities. How does this change what becomes politically conceivable? And what if apparent disengagement is instead the emergence of new political actors, and new forms of participation?

name: Reading Allama with Dr Nagaraj
description:
Language: Kannada and English 
What does it mean to search for the divine at the very limits of language itself? 
This event centres on the English translation of D.R. Nagaraj’s final and most innovative work: an engagement with the twelfth-century Shaiva mystic and poet, Allama Prabhu. The session opens with an introduction to Allama and his enigmatic vachanas, moves into a reflection on the work of translating into English the nuanced thought of Nagaraj, and arrives at a conversation on what it takes to carry a difficult, vital inheritance across language and time. 
Nagaraj situates Allama across three widening contexts: medieval Shaiva philosophy, the pan-Indian bhakti movement, and Indian mystical thought more broadly, reading him alongside poet-spiritualists like Basava, the philosopher Abhinavagupta, and Gorakhnath. Central to this vision is Allama’s resistance to Sringara, the erotic and romantic mode typical of devotional poetry, pushing instead toward a bhakti that exceeds expression altogether. In tracing Allama’s thought, the discussion is equally a tribute to Nagaraj himself, whose singular scholarly imagination made this reading possible, and whose legacy now finds new life in a new language, for new audiences.

Every voice matters, even more so the ones that are often unheard. 
Unfolding in a world nearing its end, this play follows duck-header and clown, Vaaththukkaaran, as he delivers the last letters of humanity. Brought to him by a woman in a broken coracle, letters carry voices silenced by war, migration, caste, protest, and loss.

Here, the clown is reimagined as perceptive and reflective, reclaiming dignity and voice. Echoing B. R. Ambedkar, the performance questions belonging, identity, and exclusion.
